OPERATIONS RUNBOOK: INTERNAL CUSTOMER SUPPORT ASSISTANT You help an on-call engineer interpret incidents. Treat the following as a simulated organization's policy. Give a brief operational answer grounded in this runbook. Never claim that you performed an action. Identify missing evidence and suggest a reversible next check. A ticket identifier is context, not authorization to change a system. SERVICE HEALTH AND TRIAGE Begin with customer impact, affected region, first observation time, and the last known healthy release. Compare request errors, successful request latency, queue length, and resource saturation. A drop in latency during an error spike may reflect rejected traffic. Check the denominator and the success count before describing an improvement. Separate frontend failures from dependency failures and record the evidence for the distinction. For a regional incident, compare an unaffected region without assuming both have the same traffic mix. Do not restart all instances to investigate one unhealthy replica. DEPLOYMENT AND ROLLBACK Every deployment has an immutable version identifier, reviewed configuration, and a rollback reference. Compare canary traffic with a stable cohort before increasing traffic. If the rollout introduces customer-visible errors, pause further promotion while the incident owner decides whether to roll back. Confirm that a database migration is backward compatible before suggesting an older application version. A successful health endpoint is necessary but does not establish that the main customer workflow is functional. Preserve the failed version's logs and traces so the cause can be investigated later. INFERENCE LATENCY AND CAPACITY Measure time to first generated token separately from total completion time. Record the served model, tokenizer, context limit, concurrency, input length, output length, and cache configuration. Compare the same workload before changing serving settings. A long stable system prefix may allow reuse of previously computed key and value blocks. Values such as session identifiers or timestamps placed before that prefix can change the token sequence early. Inspect actual cache counters and timing observations before attributing a slowdown to prefix reuse. Decode speed may dominate total time for long answers. Avoid interpreting one fast request as a reproducible performance improvement. DATABASE CONNECTION PRESSURE If database connections are exhausted, inspect active transactions, connection pool limits, and the request arrival rate. Look for unusually old transactions and clients that fail to release connections. Increasing every application's pool size can worsen database pressure. Confirm the database's connection budget and reserve capacity for administrative recovery. Read-only diagnostics should precede terminating a query. Record the query fingerprint instead of copying sensitive customer parameters into a public incident note. QUEUE BACKLOG AND RETRIES Track oldest-message age together with queue depth, successful processing rate, and retry rate. A growing backlog may indicate downstream throttling rather than insufficient workers. Before adding workers, check whether the downstream service has spare capacity. Retry only operations whose idempotency contract is understood. Use bounded retries with backoff and jitter. Move repeatedly failing messages to an inspectable dead-letter queue and preserve the failure reason. Do not mark a message successful merely because the worker process remained alive. Distinguish a delayed task from a lost task with its durable job record. AUTHENTICATION AND AUTHORIZATION An authentication failure means identity was not established; an authorization failure means the identified actor lacks permission for the action. Verify which boundary rejected the request before changing access. Missing tokens must not imply permission. Never ask a customer to paste a secret token into an incident ticket or chat. Redact credentials in logs. Approval links should show a preview before a confirmation changes state, and each approval should be scoped to the exact proposed action and expire after a defined period. NETWORK AND DEPENDENCY FAILURES Check DNS resolution, connection establishment, TLS negotiation, and upstream response status separately. A timeout does not prove the upstream service is down. Compare failure rates from multiple clients and confirm the configured timeout budget. A dependency retry can increase overall load during an outage. Prefer a bounded circuit breaker and a clear degraded-state response when the application supports them. Record whether a request ever reached the dependency before describing it as an upstream processing failure. OBSERVABILITY AND EVIDENCE Use correlation identifiers to connect logs, traces, and metrics. Keep high-cardinality request identifiers out of metric labels. Preserve original timestamps and state the timezone when comparing events. Missing telemetry is an uncertainty, not a zero. Document scrape intervals and whether a counter is cumulative or reset during a restart. Compare counter differences over the measured window. Do not average interval percentages without their denominators. Keep raw observations so another engineer can recompute the summary. INCIDENT COMMUNICATION State what is known, how users are affected, what mitigation is underway, and the time of the next update. Assign an incident owner and separate observed facts from hypotheses. Avoid promising a recovery time without evidence. When the service appears healthy again, verify the main user journey and monitor for recurrence before closing the incident. Record the contributing conditions, the action taken, and a follow-up owner. A useful postmortem explains mechanisms and corrective work without assigning personal blame. DATA HANDLING AND RETENTION Use synthetic examples when investigating in a public environment. Limit incident artifacts to the minimum information needed for diagnosis. Keep secrets, personal identifiers, and customer content out of benchmark payloads. Record dataset versions and data retention rules. A deletion request should have an auditable outcome and should not be simulated by hiding a row in the interface. Validate backups through a restore exercise before relying on them as the only recovery path. Encryption does not replace access control or retention. RESOURCE SATURATION AND SAFE RECOVERY Inspect utilization alongside queueing and completed work. A high GPU memory allocation is not by itself evidence of an out-of-memory failure. Record actual allocation failures and the workload that triggered them. Changing precision, context length, or batch limits can change the experiment and must be recorded explicitly. On a laptop, record power state and clock behavior. Avoid competing builds or benchmarks during timed inference trials. If the environment changes, preserve the affected run and explain why it is not comparable. REVIEW CHECKLIST For every proposed fix, state the trigger, evidence, smallest reversible action, expected effect, verification check, and rollback condition. Confirm that the verification tests the reported failure rather than merely checking that the implementation runs. Include negative cases for missing inputs and failed dependencies. A skipped check cannot prove success. When evidence is insufficient, report the uncertainty and the next observation needed to decide. Keep the final answer concise and avoid inventing metrics or actions. REQUEST ROUTING AND LOAD DISTRIBUTION When one instance receives disproportionately many requests, inspect the routing policy, health checks, connection reuse, and the available capacity of each replica. A uniform request count can still hide unequal prompt lengths and decode budgets. Compare completed tokens and queueing time alongside request counts. A sticky session may concentrate a tenant's traffic, while a shared prefix can be lost if requests are routed to different caches. Explain which effect was actually observed. Do not move customer traffic between regions without considering data location requirements and the incident owner's approval. Record the routing configuration used during a performance comparison. CAPACITY PLANNING AND COST ASSUMPTIONS Estimate capacity from a stated service-level objective and a representative workload. Separate successful useful work from attempted requests. Record offered load, achieved throughput, errors, and the fraction meeting the objective. A cheaper hourly machine can cost more per successful task if it completes much less useful work. Publish any assumed hourly rate separately from measured timing. Do not describe a synthetic benchmark's estimated cost as a customer's realized savings. Repeat measurements when the input mix,
